title: Akshay Kumar and Priyadarshan Proved Everyone Wrong: Bhooth Bangla Crosses ₹175 Crore
excerpt: The horror comedy that reunited Bollywood's greatest comedy partnership has now earned ₹248 crore worldwide, becoming Kumar's biggest hit in five years and his 12th film past ₹200 crore
body:
The Comeback Nobody Saw Coming

Let's be honest: if you'd told anyone two years ago that Akshay Kumar's next big hit would be a horror comedy directed by Priyadarshan, they would have nodded politely and changed the subject. After a brutal stretch of underperformers — Selfiee, Bade Miyan Chote Miyan, Khel Khel Mein — the consensus on Kumar had calcified into something uncomfortably close to a eulogy. The superstar era was over. The box office magic had faded. Time to pivot to character roles.

Then Bhooth Bangla walked in, cracked its knuckles, and reminded everyone that writing off Akshay Kumar is a historically terrible idea.

The horror comedy, which released on April 17, has now crossed ₹175 crore nett in India and ₹248 crore worldwide after 30 days of release, with $5.4 million in overseas collections. Day 30 alone brought in ₹1.25 crore — a 48% jump from Friday — and the film is tracking comfortably toward a ₹180 crore nett finish. It's Akshay Kumar's 12th film to cross ₹200 crore worldwide, and comfortably his biggest hit since Sooryavanshi in 2021.

The Priyadarshan Effect

The numbers tell one story. The why tells a better one.

Priyadarshan returning to direct Kumar is not just a reunion — it's a homecoming. This is the partnership that gave us Hera Pheri (2000), Bhool Bhulaiyaa (2007), Bhagam Bhag (2006), and Garam Masala (2005). For an entire generation, these weren't just comedies — they were the comedies. The ones you watched on pirated DVDs at your cousin's house during summer holidays. The ones whose dialogues you can still recite at 2 AM after three drinks.

Bhooth Bangla taps directly into that nostalgia while updating the formula. The horror-comedy genre — which Priyadarshan essentially pioneered in Hindi cinema with Bhool Bhulaiyaa — gets a fresh coat of paint with better VFX, a tighter screenplay, and a supporting cast led by the incomparable Tabu and the eternally scene-stealing Paresh Rawal. The three of them together generate the kind of chemistry that scripts can set up but only genuine performer magic can deliver.

The Box Office Breakdown

Let's crunch the numbers for the data nerds (and we know you're out there, refreshing Sacnilk at midnight):

  • Week 1: ₹94.85 crore nett — a massive opening that signalled genuine audience hunger
  • Week 2: Held strong with minimal drops, unusual for a comedy
  • Week 3-4: Leggy run driven by word-of-mouth and repeat viewings
  • Day 30: ₹1.25 crore (₹0.85 crore on Friday → 48% Saturday jump)
  • India Total: ₹175.35 crore nett
  • Worldwide: ₹248 crore (approximately $29.5 million)
  • Overseas: $5.4 million

That overseas number deserves its own paragraph. $5.4 million for a Hindi horror comedy — not a Yash Raj tentpole, not a Marvel-scale VFX spectacle — is remarkable. It reflects exactly what anyone who's been to a Bollywood screening in New Jersey, Brampton, or Southall could tell you: NRI audiences show up in force when the product is right. And a Kumar-Priyadarshan horror comedy is the definition of "right product" for the diaspora crowd.

The NRI Group Watch Phenomenon

There's something about horror comedies that works uniquely well in diaspora communities. Maybe it's the communal nature of the experience — screaming at jump scares, laughing at the comic relief, arguing about whether that was actually scary. Bhooth Bangla is reportedly performing particularly well in weekend evening shows across North America, the traditional "desi group outing" slot.

It's also become a three-generation film in a way few Bollywood releases manage. The grandparents come for Akshay Kumar and nostalgia. The parents come for Priyadarshan and Paresh Rawal. The kids come because their parents promised pizza after. Everyone leaves happy.

What's Next for Kumar

At ₹175 crore and climbing, Bhooth Bangla doesn't just mark a hit — it marks a recalibration. Kumar's recent misfires weren't about declining stardom; they were about mismatched material. Give the man the right director, the right genre, and the right ensemble, and the audience will come.

The film's success will almost certainly greenlight Bhooth Bangla 2 (Priyadarshan has reportedly already discussed concepts), and it restores Kumar to the A-list conversation at a time when Bollywood's box office hierarchy is being actively rewritten by younger stars. At 58, Akshay Kumar just reminded the industry that the King of Comedy never actually abdicated. He was just waiting for the right haunted house to walk into.

Horror comedies drive the 'desi group outing' phenomenon in North America. Three-generation appeal makes it a rare whole-family cinema experience for immigrant households.
